name: Machine Learning Engineering
guide:
Machine Learning Engineering is the discipline that takes a model out of a notebook and turns it into a service that runs in production at scale. Day to day, a machine learning engineer builds the pipelines that move data into training runs, writes the code that trains and fine-tunes models, and packages that model so an application can call it reliably. Much of the daily work today, based on the postings we track, centers on large language models, retrieval-augmented generation, and fine-tuning existing models rather than training from scratch. The job also includes writing tests, reviewing pull requests, and debugging why a model's output looks wrong once it is live.

This work differs from Data Science and Analytics, where the daily focus is exploring data, running experiments, and producing an insight or a one-off model rather than a shipped system. It differs from Machine Learning Operations and Infrastructure, which owns the platform underneath, the GPU clusters, deployment pipelines, and monitoring dashboards, rather than the model code itself. And it differs from AI Research, which is closer to inventing new architectures and training methods and is judged on papers and benchmarks rather than a production release. A useful way to tell the postings apart is to look at the verbs, an engineering role says build, deploy, and maintain, while a research role says investigate, publish, or advance the state of the art.

Credentials in this field are mixed. A bachelor's degree in computer science, engineering, mathematics, or a related quantitative field is the baseline most employers expect, and a master's degree becomes more common as postings move toward Senior, Staff, and Principal titles in our data. We did not find named certifications, such as a specific AWS or Google Cloud credential, stated as a requirement across the postings we sampled, so treat any cloud certification as a resume booster rather than a gatekeeper. What actually opens doors is a portfolio, a shipped model, open-source contributions, or a GitHub history that shows real production code. A PhD shows up mainly in postings adjacent to AI Research, not across the bulk of the Machine Learning Engineering postings we track.

Experience requirements skew toward the middle and upper end of the ladder. In our sample, Mid-level roles are the single largest group, followed by Senior, Lead, and Staff, and postings at Manager, Principal, and Director level together outnumber true entry-level openings by a wide margin. Junior and Intern postings made up only a small slice of what we track, which tells a hiring reader that this discipline rewards people who already have a couple of production systems behind them. Two to four years of hands-on engineering experience, ideally including at least one model that reached real users, is typically what separates a Mid-level hire from someone still job hunting. By Senior and Staff, the bar shifts to ownership, running a project end to end, mentoring other engineers, and making architecture calls that the rest of the team follows.

The technical skills that show up most often in the postings we track are Python, Rust, and Scala as core languages, appearing alongside PyTorch and TensorFlow for building and training models. Cloud platforms matter heavily, with AWS, Google Cloud, and Azure all appearing frequently, usually paired with Kubernetes, Docker, CI/CD, and Terraform for getting a model into production and keeping it there. Large language model work is now a mainstream part of the job, with fine-tuning, retrieval-augmented generation, LangChain, and prompt engineering appearing regularly alongside more classic skills like reinforcement learning and model evaluation. SQL, Java, C++, TypeScript, and distributed systems knowledge round out the list, and the NIST framework shows up often enough in our data to be worth knowing if you are aiming at regulated employers like banks or government contractors. Databricks and JAX also appear frequently, a useful signal if you are targeting teams doing heavier-scale model training.

As of today, we currently track approximately 622 open postings in this discipline, out of a broader set of 2,170 Machine Learning Engineering postings in our database. Of those 2,170, 1,077 listed an actual salary figure, and among that group the typical range ran from roughly $142,000 toward the lower end to about $222,000 toward the higher end, with some outlying postings well above and below that band. The employers we see posting most often for this discipline are Capital One, Bespoke Labs, ServiceNow, Waymo, and Crowe, followed by OpenAI, Databricks, Booz Allen Hamilton, Scale AI, and Writer. That mix, a large bank, a consulting and defense contractor, a self-driving car company, and several AI labs, shows how far this discipline has spread past pure tech companies. If you are targeting this role, the postings we track suggest aiming your resume at Mid-level through Senior first, since that is where the bulk of current hiring actually sits.
